subject: Automotive & EVs
title: IndyCar and Open-Wheel Speed
description: A micro-lesson that makes IndyCar and Open-Wheel Speed usable.

hook.text: IndyCar races are the fastest closed-circuit events in the world, with cars topping 240 mph on ovals.

buildup.text: Open-wheel cars have exposed tires and massive downforce, making them faster but more fragile than stock cars.

discovery.text: The Indy 500 alone draws over 300,000 spectators—the largest single-day attendance in all of sports.

twist.text: A bitter split between CART and IRL in 1996 nearly destroyed American open-wheel racing entirely.

climax.text: The series reunified in 2008 and has slowly rebuilt, but it still lives in F1 and NASCAR's shadow.

punchline.text: America's fastest series almost killed itself with politics.

quiz.question: What top speed can IndyCars reach on oval circuits?

details.summary: IndyCar racing features high-speed open-wheel competition on American ovals and road courses, with cars reaching over 240 mph on superspeedways and offering some of the closest racing in motorsport.
details.whyItMatters: IndyCar's unique mix of oval and road course racing demands versatile engineering and driving skill. The series produces thrilling competition and has been a proving ground for American racing talent.
takeaways: Cars exceed 240 mph on oval superspeedways
The series races on ovals, road courses, and street circuits
Pack racing on ovals creates dramatic and unpredictable finishes

faq.question: How is IndyCar different from Formula One?
faq.answer: IndyCar uses a spec chassis for closer competition and races on ovals, while F1 allows fully custom cars and races only on road and street circuits. IndyCar emphasizes close racing; F1 emphasizes engineering arms races.

faq.question: Why do IndyCar races on ovals produce such close finishes?
faq.answer: Drafting in the slipstream of other cars allows competitors to stay close at over 220 mph. Position changes happen constantly in the final laps, sometimes with winning margins under a tenth of a second.
